# {.section-divider}

::: {.part-num}
PART I
:::

::: {.rule}
:::

## What is an antibody? {.section-divider}

::: {.lede}
The precision instrument the immune system uses to tell self from non-self.
:::

## A Y-shaped protein with a vast vocabulary *(roughly 10¹⁵ words)* {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 1 · the antibody as molecule
:::

The immune system's job is to distinguish *self* from *non-self* — and to neutralize anything foreign. Antibodies are how it does that.

- An antibody is a **Y-shaped protein** produced by B cells, with two binding sites at the tips of the Y.
- Each binding site recognizes a specific molecular target — an **antigen**.
- The actual region of the antigen contacted is called an **epitope**: typically just 5–20 amino acids.

::: {.two-col .narrow-left}

::: {}

Antibodies are generated through quasi-random recombination and mutation. The immune system can, in principle, produce an astronomically large diversity of binding specificities. This is not a bug — it is how the system stays ready for anything.

:::

::: {.stat-box}
::: {.num}
~10¹⁵
:::
::: {.cap}
unique antibodies the immune system can, in principle, produce
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The ~10^15 number is theoretical diversity, not observed circulating diversity at any moment — but it sets the scale for why the immune repertoire can plausibly cover almost anything the organism will encounter.
:::

# {.section-divider}

::: {.part-num}
PART II
:::

::: {.rule}
:::

## From DNA to antibodies and antigens {.section-divider}

::: {.lede}
The same biological process produces both the recogniser and the recognised — and this is what makes everything measurable.
:::

## The central dogma is the starting point {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 2 · DNA → RNA → peptide → protein
:::

Both antibodies and antigens are proteins, and proteins are the end product of one fundamental process: **DNA is transcribed into RNA, which is translated into a chain of amino acids — a peptide — which folds into a functional protein.**

```{=html}
<div class="diagram">
<svg viewBox="0 0 900 130" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="IBM Plex Sans">
  <!-- Four boxes with thin outlines, editorial style -->
  <g stroke="#1B1A17" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none">

    <rect x="250" y="30" width="170" height="70"/>

  </g>

  <g stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1.5" fill="#6B2E2A">
    <line x1="195" y1="65" x2="245" y2="65"/>

```

::: {.callout}
[Peptide vs protein]{.label}
A **peptide** is a short amino acid chain; a **protein** is a longer, folded one. The distinction is one of length and structural complexity, not kind. Antigens and antibodies are both proteins — what differs is their origin, function, and the immune logic that connects them.
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide exists to anchor a key idea later: because the whole chain runs through DNA, every step is in principle addressable with sequencing. The peptide/protein distinction will matter when we discuss peptide-tile libraries vs full-length ORFeome libraries.
:::

## What is an antigen? {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 3 · what the immune system sees
:::

An antigen is any molecule — almost always a protein or a fragment of one — that the immune system can recognize and respond to. Antigens come from:

- **Pathogens.** Viral coat proteins, bacterial surface proteins, toxins.
- **The host itself.** In autoimmunity, the immune system generates antibodies against its own proteins.
- **Environmental sources.** Allergens such as pollen, food proteins, and other exogenous triggers.

The immune system does *not* respond to a whole protein uniformly. It responds to specific regions of that protein — **epitopes** — typically short 5–20 amino acid stretches that happen to be physically accessible and structurally recognizable.

::: {.callout}
[The single most important point]{.label}
Antibody reactivity is fundamentally a **peptide-level phenomenon** — even when the antigen presented is a full-length protein.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the conceptual hinge for everything downstream — if reactivity lives at the peptide level, then library design naturally moves toward peptide tiles, and the analysis problem becomes one of aggregating evidence across tiles that share an underlying epitope.
:::

## What is an antibody, molecularly speaking? {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 4 · how diversity is generated
:::

An antibody is a protein, encoded in DNA, produced by B cells. The remarkable thing is that the genes encoding the **antigen-binding region** are not fixed in the germline. They are assembled on the fly.

### V(D)J recombination

Gene segments are randomly shuffled and joined.

```{=html}
<div class="diagram" style="margin: 0.4em 0;">
<svg viewBox="0 0 480 90" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="IBM Plex Sans">
  <!-- V D J segments -->
  <g stroke="#1B1A17" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none">
    <rect x="20"  y="20" width="60" height="35"/>
    <rect x="110" y="20" width="40" height="35"/>
    <rect x="180" y="20" width="60" height="35"/>
  </g>
  <text x="50"  y="43" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-size="18" font-weight="500" fill="#1B1A17">V</text>
  <text x="130" y="43" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-size="18" font-weight="500" fill="#1B1A17">D</text>
  <text x="210" y="43" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-size="18" font-weight="500" fill="#1B1A17">J</text>
  <text x="130" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono" font-size="10" fill="#4A4742">germline gene segments</text>
  <!-- Arrow to recombined -->
  <g stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1.5" fill="#6B2E2A">
    <line x1="255" y1="37" x2="305" y2="37"/>
    <polygon points="305,37 298,33 298,41"/>
  </g>
  <text x="280" y="25" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono" font-size="9" fill="#6B2E2A">recombine</text>
  <!-- Joined product -->
  <g stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none">
    <rect x="320" y="20" width="140" height="35"/>
  </g>
  <text x="390" y="43" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-size="14" font-style="italic" font-weight="500" fill="#6B2E2A">V—D—J</text>
  <text x="390" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono" font-size="10" fill="#4A4742">unique combination</text>
</svg>
</div>
```

### …then somatic mutation and selection

Rounds of mutation refine binding affinity in response to antigen exposure across the organism's lifetime.

::: {.callout}
[Why the reactome is biographical]{.label}
The antibody sequence is partly determined by the genome and partly by a stochastic, exposure-driven process happening within the lifetime of the organism. This is what makes the antibody reactome **biographically informative** in a way the genome alone is not.
:::

## How the DNA → peptide → protein chain enables measurement {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 5 · the bookkeeping is DNA throughout
:::

Because every protein — including every antigen — is ultimately encoded in DNA, the whole experimental chain is in principle addressable with sequencing.

1. **Design the antigen library *in silico*.** Take any set of protein sequences (a human proteome, all known viral proteins, a set of allergens); tile them into overlapping peptides; synthesize the corresponding DNA sequences computationally.
2. **Express the proteins from that DNA.** Cell-free transcription and translation produce the actual peptide or protein library in the lab.
3. **Attach a unique DNA barcode to each library member.** This is what MIPSA does via its self-assembly mechanism — covalently linking a DNA identifier to each expressed protein.
4. **Read out by sequencing.** When antibodies in a sample bind their target antigens, those antigens (and their attached barcodes) are pulled down. Sequencing the barcodes tells you *which* antigens were bound, and in what quantities.

::: {.callout}
[The foundational insight]{.label}
The **measurement currency is DNA throughout** — from library design, to barcoding, to readout. The biology happens in the middle (proteins binding proteins), but the experimental bookkeeping is entirely nucleotide-based. An immunological binding experiment becomes a sequencing experiment.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is *the* slide for MIPSA's existence. Everything else in the platform follows from the fact that you can encode the antigen library, the barcoding, and the readout in DNA throughout — making the whole thing compatible with high-throughput sequencing infrastructure.
:::

# {.section-divider}

::: {.part-num}
PART III
:::

::: {.rule}
:::

## What is the antibody reactome? {.section-divider}

::: {.lede}
Not a blueprint, not what's being expressed — a record of exposures and responses.
:::

## A snapshot of immunological history {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 6 · defining the reactome
:::

The **antibody reactome** is the complete set of antigen-binding reactivities present in a biological sample — typically blood serum or plasma — at a given point in time.

::: {.two-col .narrow-left}

::: {}

Think of it as a snapshot of immunological history:

- every pathogen encountered,
- every vaccine received,
- every self-protein the immune system has mistakenly targeted,
- every allergen that has triggered a response.

If the genome is the **blueprint** and the transcriptome is **what's being expressed**, the reactome is something different — it's a **record of exposures and responses**, written in the language of binding specificities.

:::

::: {}

For a data scientist, the useful framing is concrete:


# {.section-divider}

::: {.part-num}
PART IV
:::

::: {.rule}
:::

## Why is it interesting? {.section-divider}

::: {.lede}
Four reasons the reactome is worth measuring — and one reason it's hard.
:::

## An omic with memory {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 7 · why durability matters
:::

Unlike gene expression, which fluctuates with conditions, antibody reactivities are relatively **durable**. An infection years ago can leave a detectable antibody signature today.

```{=html}
<div class="diagram">
<svg viewBox="0 0 760 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="IBM Plex Sans">
  <!-- Gene expression panel -->
  <text x="20" y="22" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-size="14" font-weight="500" fill="#1B1A17">Gene expression</text>
  <text x="20" y="38" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-style="italic" font-size="11" fill="#4A4742">fluctuates with conditions</text>
  <line x1="20" y1="80" x2="720" y2="80" stroke="#B8AE94" stroke-width="0.75"/>
  <polyline points="20,80 60,65 100,90 140,60 180,92 220,68 260,85 300,62 340,88 380,72 420,84 460,65 500,90 540,68 580,85 620,72 660,82 700,76 720,80"
            fill="none" stroke="#4A4742" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <!-- Reactome panel -->
  <text x="20" y="118" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-size="14" font-weight="500" fill="#6B2E2A">Antibody reactome</text>
  <text x="20" y="134" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-style="italic" font-size="11" fill="#4A4742">durable — exposures leave persistent signatures</text>
  <line x1="20" y1="180" x2="720" y2="180" stroke="#B8AE94" stroke-width="0.75"/>
  <polyline points="20,180 220,180 220,160 460,160 460,140 720,140"
            fill="none" stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="2"/>
  <!-- Exposure markers -->
  <circle cx="220" cy="180" r="5" fill="#E8C547" stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1"/>
  <circle cx="460" cy="160" r="5" fill="#E8C547" stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="220" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono" font-size="9" fill="#4A4742">↑ exposure</text>
  <text x="460" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono" font-size="9" fill="#4A4742">↑ exposure</text>
  <text x="740" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-family="IBM Plex Mono" font-size="9" fill="#4A4742">time →</text>
</svg>
</div>
```

::: {.callout}
[Unusual among omics]{.label}
The reactome carries **longitudinal information in a cross-sectional measurement**. A single blood draw, in principle, encodes years of immunological history.
:::

## It encodes exposure history at population scale {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 8 · the epidemiological signal
:::

At the population level, the reactome is a rich epidemiological signal. Patterns of reactivity across individuals reveal:

- **Pathogen exposure.** Which pathogens has a community been exposed to? Reactivity patterns across individuals reveal community-level infection histories.
- **Vaccine effectiveness.** Which vaccines are working? Antibody signatures track real-world immune response, not just intended response.
- **Demographic clustering.** How do immune responses cluster across age, geography, and other demographic groups?

::: {.callout}
[The framing]{.label}
A cross-sectional cohort measurement of the antibody reactome is, in effect, a longitudinal sero-epidemiology study compressed into a single time point.
:::

::: {.notes}
The implication for study design is that you can extract a great deal of exposure-history information from a comparatively modest cohort without needing the years of follow-up that a traditional longitudinal design would require.
:::

## It can detect disease — including before symptoms {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 9 · autoantibodies and early detection
:::

**Autoantibodies** — antibodies that mistakenly target the body's own proteins — are associated with a wide range of diseases: lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, certain cancers, and many others. In some cases they appear **years before clinical diagnosis**, making the reactome a candidate for early detection.

```{=html}
<div class="diagram">
<svg viewBox="0 0 720 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="IBM Plex Sans">
  <!-- Main timeline -->
  <line x1="60" y1="90" x2="660" y2="90" stroke="#1B1A17" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <!-- Early marker -->
  <circle cx="160" cy="90" r="8" fill="#E8C547" stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="160" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-size="13" font-weight="500" fill="#1B1A17">autoantibodies</text>
  <text x="160" y="76" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-size="13" font-weight="500" fill="#1B1A17">appear</text>
  <!-- Late marker -->

  <text x="520" y="76" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Serif" font-size="13" font-weight="500" fill="#1B1A17">diagnosis</text>

```

::: {.callout}
[Why this matters clinically]{.label}
Autoantibody signatures move the detectable disease state earlier on the timeline — opening the possibility of intervention before clinical symptoms manifest. This is the promise; the data problem is what makes it hard.
:::

## It is a hard measurement problem {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Slide 10 · the data challenge
:::

Until recently, measuring the antibody reactome comprehensively was not feasible. Protein microarrays could probe thousands of antigens but were expensive and limited in content. The real breakthrough came with **sequencing-based display methods** — PhIP-Seq, and more recently MIPSA — which probe hundreds of thousands of antigens simultaneously across many samples.

### What makes the data problem genuinely interesting

- A **very wide matrix** — hundreds of thousands of antigens.
- A **moderate number of samples** — far fewer than antigens.
- **Extreme sparsity** — most cells are zero or near-zero.
- **Heavy-tailed count distributions** — far from Gaussian.
- A **background noise structure** that must be estimated from **mock-IP controls** run alongside every experiment.

::: {.callout}
[Looking ahead]{.label}
These are exactly the kinds of problems where the choice of statistical framework matters — and where assumptions, if left unexamined, can quietly corrupt the results. Section 5 takes up the **probe-aggregation problem** that follows from this structure.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a natural endpoint for Sections 1–4. The material on probe aggregation, the RMA analogy, and the negative-binomial framing belongs in a Section-5 follow-on deck. We've set the stage: the reactome is biologically interesting, technologically newly accessible, and statistically non-trivial.
:::

## From plasma to a count matrix {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
the assay workflow
:::

```{=html}
<div class="diagram">
<svg viewBox="0 0 900 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <defs>
    <marker id="arF2" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="10" refX="8" refY="3" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L8,3 L0,6 z" fill="#6B2E2A"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

    <text x="60"  y="98" font-size="9" fill="#4A4742">~10&#8308; protein-DNA</text>

    <line x1="110" y1="90" x2="128" y2="90" stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arF2)"/>

    <rect x="130" y="60" width="120" height="60" rx="3" fill="#ECE6D7" stroke="#1B1A17" stroke-width="1"/>
    <text x="190" y="78">Mix with plasma</text>

    <line x1="390" y1="90" x2="408" y2="90" stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arF2)"/>

    <rect x="410" y="60" width="100" height="60" rx="3" fill="#ECE6D7" stroke="#1B1A17" stroke-width="1"/>

    <line x1="510" y1="90" x2="528" y2="90" stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arF2)"/>

    <rect x="530" y="60" width="100" height="60" rx="3" fill="#ECE6D7" stroke="#1B1A17" stroke-width="1"/>

    <line x1="630" y1="90" x2="648" y2="90" stroke="#6B2E2A" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arF2)"/>

```

- **One IP per sample** pulls down the antibodies in that plasma and whatever library members they bound.
- **Mock IPs** (no plasma) run alongside give the per-experiment background — what sticks to the beads regardless of sample.
- Final readout is a familiar **count matrix**: rows = library members (UCIs), columns = samples, entries = sequencing reads.

## The library is the universe {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Limitation 1 · what can the assay see?
:::

- A MIPSA experiment can only detect antibodies against antigens that are **in the library**.
- Library design decisions are upstream of everything:
  - Which proteome(s)? Human ORFeome only? Plus viral, bacterial, allergens, tumour antigens?
  - Which **isoforms**? Most libraries carry one canonical isoform per gene.
  - **Splicing variants, fusion proteins, mutant epitopes** are not present unless explicitly designed in.
- Anything not in the library is invisible — and there is no "no signal" inference you can draw about absent antigens.

::: {.callout}
[The most common over-interpretation]{.label}
"Patient X has no antibodies against Y" usually means "the library did not include Y, or the form of Y the antibody recognises." The library catalogue is part of the result.
:::

## Linear vs conformational; native vs not {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Limitation 2 · what proteins really look like in the assay
:::

MIPSA's full-length proteins are made in a cell-free system. That improves over PhIP-Seq's short peptides — but the proteins in the tube are not the proteins in the body.

- **Most native folding probably occurs**, but it has not been systematically benchmarked for every ORF in any library. Some proteins almost certainly do not fold properly without their cellular context.
- **No post-translational modifications** in standard cell-free systems: no glycosylation, phosphorylation, citrullination, etc. Antibodies that specifically recognise a PTM (a major class of autoantibodies) will not bind their target here.
- **Membrane proteins, large multi-domain proteins, complexes** are all problematic.
- **Conformational epitopes** are *partially* recovered relative to peptide tiles, but practical coverage is library-dependent and rarely measured directly.

::: {.notes}
Be honest about uncertainty. MIPSA is a young technology and the field has not yet systematically characterised which fractions of the proteome fold correctly in its cell-free system. The right framing: better than peptide tiles for conformational coverage; how much better is an open question per library.
:::

## What the bead actually catches {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Limitation 3 · isotype and abundance
:::

- **Protein A/G beads** efficiently capture IgG, with mild subclass biases. They capture IgM, IgA, and IgE poorly.
- Most published MIPSA / PhIP-Seq studies are **IgG reactome studies** even when they don't say so explicitly.
- **Dynamic range is finite.** Each antibody binds its own cognate antigens, so high-titre antibodies don't directly "outcompete" rare ones for binding sites. But abundant antibodies (against common pathogens, vaccines) generate very large counts that consume a disproportionate share of the per-sample sequencing budget — pushing rare specificities closer to the noise floor where mock-IP controls matter most.
- **Polyreactive and "sticky" antibodies** exist and generate broad, low-specificity signals across many library members.

::: {.callout}
[A useful sanity check]{.label}
In any adult IgG dataset, look for known anti-EBV, anti-CMV, and anti-flu hits. If they're not there, something is wrong upstream.
:::

## Counts are not affinities {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Limitation 4 · what the count actually encodes
:::

A read count for a given UCI in a given sample reflects roughly:

::: {.callout}
[Count &#8733;]{.label}
(antibody concentration) &#215; (antibody affinity) &#215; (avidity) &#215; (library-member starting abundance) &#215; (1 &minus; loss during wash) &#215; (sequencing depth allocation)
:::

- Two of these — antibody concentration and antibody affinity — are confounded in any single sample.
- High counts ≠ high-affinity binding. They could just mean an abundant low-affinity antibody.
- Library-member starting abundance varies; without correction, well-represented members look like they pull more antibody than they really do.
- **Differential** counts across samples are more interpretable than absolute counts — but only after appropriate normalisation, and only between probes for the same antigen.

::: {.notes}
This is the MIPSA analogue of "density × abundance, not percentage" from the cfMeDIP-seq talk. Both are IP-based, both produce counts that are not the underlying biological quantity, both need per-feature normalisation.
:::

## Technical confounders {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
Limitation 5 · what varies between runs
:::

The PhIP-Seq literature has documented several sources of run-to-run variability — most should be expected in MIPSA too:

- **Library version and lot.** UCI representation isn't perfectly even; different library preparations may differ in which barcodes are well-represented at the start.
- **Bead lot, IP day, plasma processing.** Same considerations as any IP-based assay.
- **PCR cycles and amplification bias.** Barcode-region GC content and adapter chemistry can introduce per-barcode amplification biases.
- **Sequencing depth allocation.** Usually addressed by counts-per-million-style normalisation, but very low-depth samples remain unreliable.
- **Mock-IP variability.** Background changes per batch — so the *same* batch's mock IP is the right control, not a historical one.

::: {.callout}
[The same question as for cfMeDIP-seq]{.label}
How do technical groupings (plate, day, lot) line up with biological groupings (case, control, exposure)? If they overlap, batch effect and biology are indistinguishable.
:::

## What MIPSA simply cannot resolve {visibility="hidden"}

::: {.eyebrow}
Limitation 6 · structural blind spots
:::

- **PTM-dependent epitopes** (e.g. citrullinated antigens in rheumatoid arthritis) — invisible without a custom PTM-aware library.
- **Carbohydrate, lipid, and small-molecule antigens** — not protein, not in the library.
- **Antibodies recognising native multimeric complexes** — the cell-free system rarely assembles complexes.
- **Affinity, on-rate, off-rate** — the assay gives a single count, not a binding curve.
- **Functional consequence** (neutralising vs non-neutralising) — needs orthogonal assays (e.g. neutralisation, ADCC).

[Knowing what an assay *cannot* answer is the cheapest way to avoid over-interpreting it.]{.footnote}

## Next: actually looking at the data {.section-divider}

::: {.rule}
:::

::: {.lede}
With this design-level reading in hand, we can ask what the count matrix looks like, what the per-sample QC metrics say, which probes co-vary on the same antigen, and which patterns are real biology versus library, batch, or background.
:::

## Further reading {.smaller}

::: {.eyebrow}
References worth checking
:::

::: {.refs}

- **Credle JJ et al. (2022)** *Unbiased discovery of autoantibodies associated with severe COVID-19 via genome-scale self-assembled DNA-barcoded protein libraries.* Nat Biomed Eng 6(8):992–1003.  
  <span class="note">[The MIPSA paper.]</span>

- **Larman HB et al. (2011)** *Autoantigen discovery with a synthetic human peptidome.* Nat Biotechnol 29(6):535–541.  
  <span class="note">[The original PhIP-Seq paper.]</span>

- **Mohan D et al. (2018)** *PhIP-Seq characterization of serum antibodies using oligonucleotide-encoded peptidomes.* Nat Protoc 13(9):1958–1978.  
  <span class="note">[Practical PhIP-Seq protocol.]</span>

- **Recent PhIP-Seq reviews** in Frontiers in Bioinformatics (2024) and Molecular & Cellular Proteomics (2024) discuss methods, applications, and limitations including conformational epitopes, PTMs, and non-specific binding.

- **BEER** — Bayesian Estimation in PhIP-Seq (Chen et al.) — for detecting and quantifying reactivity in PhIP-Seq-style data. Likely adaptable to MIPSA counts.

- **edgeR** (Robinson, McCarthy, Smyth) — negative-binomial framework for count data; used for per-tile or per-UCI hit calling.

:::
